messages.subject: design of sampling units
parts:
Dear all,

We are surveying the population of guanacos (a large, wild ungulate)
in a 3600 km2 island-like peninsula in eastern Patagonia, aiming to
explain the variation in abundance due to habitat and human-related
factors. We surveyed 360 km of transects, using internal "roads"
(usually very bad, always surveyed using a 4WD pickup vehicle)
connecting different ranches across the area. In total, we traveled
along 12 different lines of variable length (between 9 and 70 km).
The explanatory factors (each with 3 levels) we are considering are:
habitat type, density of ranch-buildings and hunting pressure. Sheep
abundance will be an explanatory variable based on the estimates of
sheep encounter rate. The response variable will be guanaco encounter
rate.
As we will combine the factors with their different levels, this will
result in 9 different strata. Thus, we will consider the sampling
unit for a given stratum as the part of a long transect falling
within that stratum. Our problem is that the number of sampling units
per stratum will be too small in relation to the number of
explanatory variables/factors we want to test.
Questions are:
1. Is it valid to split the transect into smaller segments along a
line, and to consider these smaller segments as the new sampling
units?
If so, we may now face the problem of autocorrelation among the
sampling units placed along the same transect.
2. Is it possible to solve this problem by separating the new
sampling units, leaving blank spaces between them?
3. If this is ok, how can we detect and measure the autocorrelation
between smaller sampling units in order to decide their length and
the separation between contiguous units?

Any help/suggestions will be very much appreciated-

Ricardo
